You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: low frequency, mid load; Ip = 25 uA peak, f = 50 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 680 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: high frequency, small Cp, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 200 Hz, Cp = 17.5 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: low frequency, large Cp; Ip = 25 uA peak, f = 50 Hz, Cp = 32.5 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: high frequency, large Cp, heavy load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 200 Hz, Cp = 32.5 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: hot, heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 200 kOhm, temperature 85 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:

S2       2.04    2.09    83.1   0.518      6.14  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S3        4.2    4.21    23.2  0.0865      3.75  ok       FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL    
S4       1.79    1.82    57.1   0.759      3.21  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       1.74    1.74    8.96       -      20.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6       1.55    1.56    25.4       -        12  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 4 of 12.

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

Design 1 'sshi_optimized': duplicate: same structure as an earlier design (c0001); nothing new was simulated. Values are tuned automatically, so propose a different structure.

REPEATED PROBLEM: your last three designs all show the same failure: too little power reaches the output on some conditions [underpower]. Change the part of the circuit responsible for it rather than its values.

BEST DESIGNS SO FAR (values already tuned):

*   Goal: Power a sensor-node load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Requirements: $V_{out\_min} \ge 1.8\text{V}$, $V_{out\_max} \le 3.6\text{V}$, $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$, $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$, $dV \le 0.02\text{V}$.
    *   Best Design so far: `p_sshi_zener` (Score 77.12).
        *   Passes S1, S2, S3, S4, S5.
        *   Fails S6: $V_{pp} = 70\text{mV}$ (too high), $dV = 41.4\text{mV}$ (too high).
        *   S6 is "hot, heavy load" ($R_L = 200\text{k}\Omega$, $T=85^\circ\text{C}$).
    *   Problem with `p_sshi_zener`: On S6, the storage capacitor is not buffering enough (too large ripple) and hasn't settled (too large $dV$). This suggests the storage capacitor $C_1$ is too small or the energy delivery isn't quite efficient enough to overcome the heavy load while keeping ripple low. However, the tuning algorithm handles $C_1$ values. The $dV$ failure indicates the time constant $\tau = C_1 \cdot R_L$ (or similar) is causing a slow approach to equilibrium.

    *   The `p_sshi_zener` design is essentially a Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI) circuit combined with a Full Bridge Rectifier (FBR) and a Zener clamp.
    *   Wait, looking at `p_sshi_zener` components:
        *   D1-D4: Full bridge (pzp $\to$ out, pzn $\to$ out, 0 $\to$ pzp, 0 $\to$ pzn).
        *   C1: Storage capacitor on `out`.
        *   DZ1: Zener clamp on `out`.
        *   L1 and S1 (G1): Inductive flip circuit across pzp and pzn.
    *   This is a "Parallel SSHI" (P-SSHI) topology. The inductor L1 and switch S1 are in parallel with the piezo, flipping the voltage at the peaks to extract more energy.
    *   The failure on S6 (heavy load) is mainly ripple and settlement.
    *   If $C_1$ is too small, ripple is high. If $C_1$ is too large, $t_{up}$ might be too slow, or the circuit might not reach the target voltage in time. But on S6, it's specifically ripple and $dV$.
    *   The $dV$ failure ($dV = 0.041\text{V}$) means the voltage is still rising or falling between $0.6\text{s}$ and $0.8\text{s}$.
    *   The ripple failure ($70\text{mV}$) means the capacitor isn't filtering the rectifier pulses well enough.

    *   S6 has $R_L = 200\text{k}\Omega$. Power required is $1.8^2 / 200\text{k} = 16.2\text{uW}$.
    *   `p_sshi_zener` delivers $47.3\text{uW}$ on S6. Power is sufficient.

If I proposed `sshi_optimized` in Round 3 and it was a duplicate, it didn't run. The one before that might have been underpowered.

    *   Let's analyze S6: $R_L = 200\text{k}\Omega$, $T=85^\circ\text{C}$.
    *   At $85^\circ\text{C}$, DSCH diode drops might change, or the piezo leakage might increase (though the model is 20MOhm fixed).
    *   Wait, the $dV$ failure suggests it's still charging. $dV = |mean(0.7-0.8) - mean(0.6-0.7)| = 0.041\text{V}$. This is quite large. The storage capacitor $C_1$ is likely too small to stabilize the voltage quickly, but maybe too large to let it settle? No, if it's still rising, it's too large. If it's falling, it's too small.
    *   Given $V_{avg} = 3.08\text{V}$ and $V_{max} = 3.11\text{V}$, it's likely charging up to the Zener limit or the equilibrium point.

    *   How to improve power delivery and stability?
    *   Could we try a "Half-Bridge" or a "Voltage Doubler" with SSHI?
    *   Another option: a different inductor placement.
    *   Let's try an S-SSHI (Series SSHI). In S-SSHI, the inductor is placed between the piezo and the rectifier.
    *   S-SSHI Circuit:
        Piezo $\to$ Inductor $\to$ Rectifier $\to$ Cap.
        And a switch to flip the piezo voltage.
    *   Actually, let's try a "Synchronous Rectifier" if possible? The prompt allows `S` (switches) and `SYNC`.
    *   If we replace the diodes in the bridge with switches controlled by SYNC, we'd have an active bridge. But we only have 4 switches total. A full bridge needs 4 switches.
    *   Wait, can we use the switches for rectification?
        S1: pzp to out
        S2: pzn to out
        S3: out to 0 ? No.
        S4: 0 to out ? No.
    *   A synchronous rectifier is harder with only 2 SYNC controllers.

    *   Let's try a different topology: SSHI with a different inductor/switch config.
    *   Maybe a "Buck-Boost" like structure? No, that's too complex for the components.
    *   What about a "Charge Pump" based approach? (Dickson or similar).
    *   Wait, the current P-SSHI is already quite good. Let's look at the failure again: S6 ripple $70\text{mV}$, $dV = 41\text{mV}$.
    *   $V_{avg} = 3.08\text{V}$, $V_{max} = 3.11\text{V}$.
    *   The ripple $V_{pp} = 70\text{mV}$ is the peak-to-peak in the window $0.7-0.8\text{s}$.
    *   If the load is heavy ($200\text{k}\Omega$), the capacitor $C_1$ must be large enough to keep $V_{pp} < 50\text{mV}$.
    *   $\Delta V \approx \frac{I_{load} \cdot T}{C} = \frac{(3\text{V}/200\text{k}\Omega) \cdot 0.01\text{s}}{C} = \frac{1.5 \cdot 10^{-7}}{C}$.
    *   For $\Delta V < 0.05\text{V}$, $C > 3\mu\text{F}$.
    *   The `p_sshi_zener` used $C_1 = 1.24\mu\text{F}$. That explains the ripple!
    *   Why didn't the tuner use a larger $C_1$?
        Maybe because of $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$?
        $t_{up}$ is the time to reach $1.8\text{V}$.
        $V(t) \approx \frac{I_{avg}}{C} t$.
        $1.8\text{V} = \frac{I_{avg}}{C} \cdot 0.4 \implies C < \frac{I_{avg} \cdot 0.4}{1.8}$.
        On S6, $I_{avg} \approx P_{load} / V_{avg} = 47.3\text{uW} / 3.08\text{V} \approx 15.3\mu\text{A}$.
        $C < \frac{15.3\mu\text{A} \cdot 0.4}{1.8} \approx 3.4\mu\text{F}$.
        So $C=3\mu\text{F}$ should be possible.
        But $I_{avg}$ might be lower during the startup phase (before the inductor flip is efficient).

    *   The problem is the tradeoff between $t_{up}$ and ripple/settling.
    *   To fix this, we need to deliver more power *during* the startup phase or improve the efficiency of the energy transfer.

    *   Let's try a differentSSH-like topology. Maybe a "Parallel-Series" hybrid?
    *   Or, how about a "SEP" (Synchronous Electric Power) approach?
    *   Let's try an SSHI with a capacitor for flipping instead of an inductor (though that's usually called SSHC). But the goal is to use the provided components.
    *   What if we use a different rectifier?
        Instead of a full bridge, maybe a half-bridge with a center-tapped piezo? (But the piezo is just two nodes pzp, pzn).
        What about a voltage doubler (Greinacher circuit)?
        A doubler can provide higher voltage, which might help $t_{up}$ for a larger $C_1$.

    *   Greinacher (Voltage Doubler):
        D1: pzp to n1
        C1: n1 to 0
        D2: pzp to out (Wait, that's not it)
        Correct Doubler:
        D1: pzp to n1
        C1: n1 to 0
        D2: n1 to out (No)
        Let's use the standard:
        D1: pzn to n1
        C1: n1 to 0
        D2: pzp to out
        C2: out to 0
        Wait, this is for AC. The piezo is a current source.
        For a current source $I \sin(\omega t)$ in parallel with $C_p$:
        D1: pzp to n1, C1: n1 to 0 (charges $C_1$ when pzp is negative?) No.
        Let's try:
        D1: pzp to n1, C1: n1 to 0 (charges $C_1$ when pzp is positive).
        D2: n1 to out, C2: out to 0 (transfers charge when pzp is negative).
        This is a doubler.

    *   Combine Doubler with SSHI?
        P-SSHI flip circuit (L1, S1) in parallel with the piezo.
        Then the doubler extracts the energy.
        This might increase the voltage faster ($t_{up}$) and allow a larger storage cap (lower ripple).

    *   Is there a simpler way?
        The P-SSHI is already very efficient. The issue is specifically the S6 load.
        What if we use an SSHI but instead of a full bridge, we use a "Switching Rectifier"?
        Actually, we can use the switches to implement a more efficient rectifier.
        But with only 2 SYNC controllers, we can't do a full synchronous bridge.

    *   Wait! We have 2 SYNC controllers.
        G1: controls S1 for flipping.
        G2: could control S2 for rectification?
        Example:
        S2: pzp to out.
        S3: pzn to out.
        G2: edges="both", phase=...
        But we need to avoid discharging the output capacitor. Diodes are better for that unless we have a very precise SYNC.

    *   Let's try a "S-SSHI" (Series SSHI).
        In S-SSHI, the inductor is in series with the rectifier.
        Topology:
        L1: pzp to n1
        S1: n1 to pzn (flip switch, G1)
        Rectifier: n1 to out (via diodes).
        This is often more efficient than P-SSHI.

    *   Let's try to refine the P-SSHI to be more robust.
        What if we use a different storage capacitor value or a different Zener?
        No, the tuner does that.

    *   What about a "Charge Pump" with the inductor?
        Actually, let's try a "Voltage Doubler" based SSHI.
        If the output voltage is higher, the current $I_{load} = V_{out} / R_L$ increases, but the charging speed $dV/dt = I_{avg} / C$ also increases if $I_{avg}$ increases.

    *   Let's look at the `p_sshi_zener` again. It fails S6 ripple and settling.
        $V_{avg} = 3.08\text{V}$, $V_{max} = 3.11\text{V}$.
        This means it's operating near the Zener limit ($3.3\text{V}$).
        If we increase the Zener voltage? No, max is $3.6\text{V}$. DZ33 is $3.3\text{V}$.
        Wait, the `p_sshi_zener` is *too* efficient on S1-S5, hitting the Zener limit.
        On S6, it's also hitting the Zener limit ($3.08\text{V}$ is close to $3.3\text{V}$ minus diode drops).
        If it's hitting the Zener limit, it's wasting energy!
        The Zener clamp is dissipating power.
        If we remove the Zener, $V_{max}$ might exceed $3.6\text{V}$ on S3 (light load).
        S3 has $R_L = 4.7\text{M}\Omega$. $V_{avg}$ will be very high.
        So we need the Zener.

    *   Can we use a different clamp?
        Instead of a Zener, we could use a "shunt regulator" if we had the components.
        Or, we can just use the Zener and try to find a topology that handles the heavy load better.

    *   Let's try a "S-SSHI" structure.
        S-SSHI:
        L1: pzp to n1
        S1: n1 to pzn (ctrl=G1, flip)
        D1: n1 to out
        D2: pzn to out (Wait, that's not right)
        Standard S-SSHI:
        The inductor is in series with the rectifier.
        The switch is used to invert the piezo voltage.
        Let's try this:
        S1: pzp to n1 (ctrl=G1, flip)
        L1: n1 to n2
        D1: n2 to out
        D2: pzn to out
        Wait, that's not a standard topology.

    *   Let's go back to a basic, highly efficient structure.
        The "P-SSHI" is already very good. Maybe the only problem is that it's "too fast" for the tuner to find the perfect $C_1$?
        No, that's unlikely.
        Let's try a "Half-Bridge" version of SSHI to reduce diode drops.
        A full bridge has 2 diodes in the path. A half-bridge has 1.
        Half-bridge:
        D1: pzp to out
        D2: pzn to out (No, this doesn't work)
        Half-bridge needs a center-tap. We don't have one.

    *   What about a "Switching Capacitor" converter?
        Maybe a simple charge pump?
        S1: pzp to n1 (ctrl=G1)
        S2: n1 to out (ctrl=G2)
        This is too complex.

    *   Let's try a "S-SSHI" more carefully.
        L1 is in series with the rectifier.
        S1 flips the piezo.
        Circuit:
        S1: pzp to pzn (ctrl=G1, flip) - Wait, this just shorts the piezo.
        Wait, the flip in P-SSHI is: L1 in series with S1, and this pair in parallel with the piezo.
